title: Restoring ecology and health in Daurala
body: Daurala is a village near Meerut with about twelve thousand residents. In 2003 the poor health of the villagers drew the attention of civil society. The groundwater of the village had become contaminated with heavy metals because untreated wastewater from the Daurala industries was leaching into the groundwater table. A Meerut-based NGO carried out a door-to-door survey of the health of residents and prepared a report. Following the principle that the polluter pays, the NGO, the village community, people's representatives, government officials and the industries met to find sustainable solutions. The capacity of the village overhead water tank was increased and an extra 900 m pipeline was laid to supply potable water. The silted village pond was desilted so that it could hold more water and recharge the aquifers. Rainwater harvesting structures were built at different places, which helped to dilute the contaminants in the groundwater after the monsoons, and 1000 trees were planted.

title: Ramesh, a migrant welder
body: Ramesh comes from a village where he, his three brothers and their families had to survive on three acres of land. The family was deeply in debt, and Ramesh left school after Class 9. After his marriage he was further hard pressed. He was impressed by out-migrants from his village who worked in Ludhiana and sent money and consumer goods home. In 1988 he moved to Punjab with a friend and worked in a woollen factory for Rs 20 a day, struggling both with expenses and with adjusting to a new culture. He then moved to Surat, learnt welding, and has since worked for the same contractor at places such as Mumbai, Gandhi Nagar, Bharuch, Jamnagar and Talcher. He now remits about Rs 20,000 a year to his father. The money is used for daily consumption, healthcare and schooling of children, and partly for agriculture, buying land and building houses. His family's standard of living has improved, but he bears the pain of separation, as he cannot take his family with him: his job is temporary and transferable.

title: Watershed management in Jhabua
body: Jhabua district lies in the westernmost agro-climatic zone of Madhya Pradesh and is one of the most backward districts of the country, with a high concentration of tribal people, mostly Bhils. Their poverty has been made worse by the degradation of forests and land. Watershed management programmes, which recognise the links between land, water and vegetation, have been implemented here with community participation. In Sat Rundi hamlet of Karravat village in Petlawad block, each household planted and maintained one tree on the common property. The Bhils planted fodder grass on the pasture land and adopted social fencing of these lands for at least two years, planning stall feeding of cattle instead of open grazing afterwards. Before the work began, a villager from an adjoining village had encroached on the common land. The villagers called the tehsildar to ascertain the rights over the land, and they resolved the conflict by making the encroacher a member of their user group and sharing with him the benefits of greening the common pastures.
